newsitem.title: UK: British stockbroker Killik clarifies Galileo role.
newsitem.headline: British stockbroker Killik clarifies Galileo role.

text.p: British stockbroking firm Killik & Co on Thursday clarified its dealings with Galileo Group, the vehicle which was to have been used in a now discredited bid for Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS).

Galileo, an offshoot of entrepreneur Andrew Regan's Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica, failed in its takeover attempt last week when the supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group defeated it in the courts and a key backer withdrew.
Killik, a shareholder in both Galileo and Lanica, said in a statement it "condemns the use of dishonest tactics and sincerely regrets that their name has been associated with any improper behaviour".
It had not previously made any comment on the affair, which has since widened to involve Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO).
The group said it had severed all links with Regan, the 31-year-old chairman of Galileo and chief executive of Lanica, who masterminded the 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) bid attempt.
It said it was strongly influenced in its decision to recommend investment in Galileo and Lanica "by the pedigree of Lanica's advisers and other backers".
British merchant bank Hambros, which advised both Galileo and Lanica, made an unreserved apology to the 153-year-old mutually-owned CWS on Monday for its involvement in the bid.

Peter Large, the senior corporate financier at Hambros responsible for the bid, has since requested "to be relieved of his executive responsibilities for the time being" to enable him to concentrate on an internal probe into Hambros' conduct.
Hambros' climbdown followed an intense defence campaign by CWS chief executive Graham Melmoth which uncovered the leaking of confidential papers by a senior CWS manager to Regan and his backers.
Galileo said the documents were provided "voluntarily" but last week a High Court judge ruled that the case represented "a gross, wilful and disgraceful breach of confidence".
He also awarded punitive costs against Regan, Galileo chairman David Lyons, Lanica and Galileo.
But on Wednesday Galileo went into voluntary solvent liquidation and its liquidator said there were sufficient assets to repay creditors in full, and enable a return to be made to shareholders.
Killik said that when it bought Lanica and Galileo shares on behalf of 200 investors, including certain partners and staff, "no one within the firm was aware of the business to be acquired".
It also said the purchases had "fully complied with the SFA (Securities and Futures Authority) conduct of business rules".

Killik said of 281,326 shares in Lanica held by its investors, 37,372 were held by certain partners and staff. "A total of 2.0 million pounds was further invested in Galileo of which certain partners and staff invested 122,398 pounds," it added.
Galileo's intention to bid for CWS first surfaced early in February and led to the suspension of Lanica's shares at 19.5 pounds on February 10 on the London Stock Exchange.
Killik said following a request in January it was informed "of the intention to approach the CWS".

It said no one at the firm had seen any CWS confidential papers "nor were they aware that such documents were in circulation until this issue became public". The firm is now "seeking to safeguard the interests of their investors".

On Wednesday British investment bank Schroders also distanced itself from the affair, saying that its investment management arm had considered withdrawing from Galileo when the controversy first arose but was "trumped" by the fact it was wound up.

Schroders said it was purely a portfolio investor in the firms and its combined total investment was below two million pounds. Banking sources said Galileo had total assets of around 10 million pounds.

The affair is now set to rumble on in the courts, with CWS pursuing private actions against Regan, Lyons, Lanica and Galileo and the SFO probing a controversial 2.4 million pound payment to a third party in an early deal between a Regan-run firm and the CWS.
($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
